addie wagenknecht.practice_summary: Artist and technologist whose work explores surveillance, gendered labour, and the political architecture of consumer technology. Her sculptures and installations repurpose industrial and domestic tech — Roombas, drones, webcams — to expose the infrastructures of automation and visibility.
addie wagenknecht.methodology: Works through material transformation of off-the-shelf technology: uses Roombas dipped in paint as autonomous painters, disassembles drones into sculptural assemblages, stages surveillance apparatus as aesthetic object. Often collaborates with hackerspaces and open-hardware communities; publishes code alongside works.
addie wagenknecht.commons_summary: Strong open-source orientation — code and hardware schematics routinely released; founding member of Deep Lab, a feminist collaborative research group sharing methodology openly.
addie wagenknecht.governance_summary: Solo artistic practice, but embedded in collective/collaborative research groups (Deep Lab) and open-hardware communities (NYC Resistor).

amalia ulman.practice_summary: Argentine-Spanish artist whose four-month Instagram performance 'Excellences & Perfections' (2014) staged influencer femininity as fiction and was acquired as a net-art work by Tate and the Whitney. Her broader practice interrogates how platforms script identity, class aspiration, and feminised labour.
amalia ulman.methodology: Operates as author-performer: long-form durational performances across social media that blur autobiography and script, then transpose the screen material into installation and film. Combines the conventions of reality TV, telenovela, and Instagram aesthetics with critical art-history reference.
amalia ulman.commons_summary: Work lives partly on platforms she doesn't own (Instagram); institutional preservation relies on Rhizome / Tate net-art acquisition workflows.

arca.practice_summary: Venezuelan musician, producer, and multimedia artist whose production for Björk, FKA twigs, and her own records pioneered a digitally-fragmented, hyper-embodied sonic aesthetic. Her visual collaborations with Jesse Kanda extend the work into avatar, latex, and installation.
arca.methodology: Builds tracks from granular synthesis, digital glitch, and trans-embodied vocal processing. Performance is central — she stages her body as digital-analog hybrid, often with Kanda's CGI avatars. The 'KICK' five-album cycle (2020-2021) foregrounds nonbinary trans embodiment as compositional substrate.
arca.commons_summary: Work is primarily commercial (major-label music), though audio-visual collaborations often released across open performance contexts.
arca.governance_summary: Solo artist with major-label relationships (XL Recordings) and long-term creative partners.

beeple.practice_summary: Mike Winkelmann's daily 3D-rendering practice 'Everydays', begun 2007 and uninterrupted since, became the substrate for 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days', sold at Christie's for $69M in 2021. That sale forced every major contemporary-art institution to revise its position on digital art and NFTs. His subsequent work spans monumental installation, the Beeple Studios exhibition space in Charleston, and continued daily renders.
beeple.methodology: One finished 3D render per day, every day, using Cinema 4D and Octane. Images are often satirical-political, drawing on current events, corporate iconography, and apocalyptic landscape. Stores and mints selected works as NFTs; also produces physical installation using kinetic sculpture and screens.
beeple.commons_summary: Early work was given freely online (Creative Commons attribution); current market practice is commercial/NFT-gated. Source files for some Everydays have been released.
beeple.governance_summary: Sole practitioner, now operating Beeple Studios as an institution-scale venue in Charleston, SC.

ben fry.practice_summary: Co-creator with Casey Reas of the Processing programming language (2001), and founder of Fathom Information Design. His own artistic practice in data visualisation treats information as an aesthetic and critical medium, not neutral illustration.
ben fry.methodology: Builds tools first, art second — Processing, Fathom's custom dataviz stack. Works from primary datasets (genomes, game code, consumer-product histories) and designs readings rather than imposing chart conventions. MIT Media Lab / Aesthetics + Computation Group lineage.
ben fry.commons_summary: Processing released under LGPL/GPL; one of the most significant commons contributions in digital art. Foundational to the creative-coding open-source ecosystem.
ben fry.governance_summary: Processing Foundation (501(c)(3) US non-profit) provides formal governance for the language; Fathom is a commercial studio. Fry holds dual practitioner/infrastructure-steward role.

charles csuri.practice_summary: American artist often cited as a founder of computer art. His 1966 'Sine Curve Man' was among the first computer-generated artworks exhibited internationally, and he built computer graphics programmes at Ohio State University that trained generations of practitioners.
charles csuri.methodology: Programmed FORTRAN on IBM mainframes in the mid-1960s, using mathematical transformations to warp figurative drawings. Later developed real-time 3D animation tools at OSU's ACCAD. Practice spans analogue painting, 2D computer graphics, 3D animation, and print.
charles csuri.commons_summary: Academic practice; code and methods published via SIGGRAPH and OSU. ACCAD continues as institutional infrastructure.
charles csuri.governance_summary: University-based practice; founded ACCAD (Advanced Computing Center for the Arts and Design) at Ohio State.

cory arcangel.practice_summary: American artist working across hacked games, browser art, performance, and print since the late 1990s. 'Super Mario Clouds' (2002) — a hacked NES cartridge displaying only scrolling clouds — became a canonical work of contemporary computer-based art and the Whitney's first game-hack acquisition.
cory arcangel.methodology: Modifies consumer technology (game cartridges, Photoshop gradients, default fonts) into conceptual gestures. The gesture is often smaller than the production around it — releases custom hardware, writes manuals, publishes books. Associated early with the Beige Programming Ensemble circuit-bending collective.
cory arcangel.commons_summary: Work often distributed online as free downloads (Cory Arcangel Studio website); methodology documented publicly. Also sells editioned gallery work commercially.
cory arcangel.governance_summary: Solo practitioner operating Cory Arcangel Studio with small staff; gallery-represented (Team Gallery, Lisson).

dmitri cherniak.practice_summary: Canadian generative artist best known for 'Ringers' (2021), a 1000-edition Art Blocks Curated series of looped string-around-pegs compositions. Practice emerged from open-source creative-coding community and pivoted to on-chain generative art.
dmitri cherniak.methodology: Writes JavaScript/p5.js algorithms designed to be minted on-chain — every token is a deterministic function of its transaction hash. Aesthetic interest in line, constraint, and emergent complexity from simple rules. Maintains close community presence via Twitter/X and Discord.
dmitri cherniak.commons_summary: Source code is often visible on-chain (verifiable via Etherscan); practice operates within the crypto-native paradigm where the algorithm is the artwork.
dmitri cherniak.governance_summary: Solo practitioner, platform-native (Art Blocks). Represented by Pace Gallery.

ed atkins.practice_summary: British artist working with CGI, motion capture, and monologue video to stage affect at the uncanny edge of synthetic embodiment. His talking-head avatars — often rendered with luxurious detail and clear digital seams — speak scripts that circle through grief, tenderness, and consumer-product abjection.
ed atkins.methodology: Writes scripts, records his own voice, then maps to off-the-shelf CGI avatars using motion capture. Deliberately keeps the simulation visible as simulation. Installation deploys multiple screens, sound, and dense print matter (books, scores).
ed atkins.commons_summary: Commercial gallery practice; work distributed through institutional/gallery channels.
ed atkins.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; represented by Cabinet London and Gladstone Gallery.

frieder nake.practice_summary: German mathematician-artist, one of the three 1965 pioneers (with Georg Nees and A. Michael Noll) whose early computer art exhibitions founded the field. Continues to teach, write, and make work as a computer-art theorist.
frieder nake.methodology: Programmed ALGOL and later graphical systems to produce plotter drawings in the 1960s. His theoretical position distinguishes between the 'surface' algorithm and the 'subface' of its material computation — a framework influential on later generative-art discourse.
frieder nake.commons_summary: Built and maintains Compart — the Center of Excellence Digital Art database at University of Bremen — a major open scholarly archive of early computer art.
frieder nake.governance_summary: Academic practice at University of Bremen; Compart operates as institutional open-access infrastructure.

golan levin.practice_summary: American artist and educator whose interactive audiovisual works and open-source toolkits have shaped two decades of creative coding. Founding director of the STUDIO for Creative Inquiry at Carnegie Mellon, where he has taught and supported a generation of new-media artists.
golan levin.methodology: Builds tools and performance systems that link gesture, sound, and image in real time. Works from the MIT Media Lab Aesthetics + Computation Group lineage (with John Maeda). Maintains the Flong archive — a widely-cited repository of creative-coding techniques and historical references.
golan levin.commons_summary: Deep commons orientation — Flong.com is a free educational resource, and Levin has contributed to Processing, openFrameworks, and p5.js ecosystems.
golan levin.governance_summary: STUDIO for Creative Inquiry at CMU (institutional), personal practice as solo artist; extensive pedagogical role.

heath bunting.practice_summary: British net.art pioneer and co-founder of the Irational.org artist network (1996), whose work interrogates the politics of identity, borders, and communication infrastructure. 'The Status Project' (ongoing) catalogues the bureaucratic procedures needed to synthesise new legal identities in the UK.
heath bunting.methodology: Treats infrastructure — passports, postal systems, mobile phones, social networks — as raw material. Early works used IRC, email, and browser hacks; later works map institutional taxonomies as diagrams. Often refuses institutional incorporation; work distributed via Irational.org.
heath bunting.commons_summary: Irational.org operates as artist-run autonomous infrastructure; work is distributed freely online and refuses standard gallery commodification.
heath bunting.governance_summary: Artist-run Irational.org collective; independent, non-institutional practice.

jesse kanda.practice_summary: Canadian-Japanese digital artist whose CGI imagery of distended, infantilised bodies shaped the visual language of Arca, FKA twigs, and Björk's late-2010s and early-2020s work. His practice sits between music video, standalone video art, and gallery installation.
jesse kanda.methodology: Works entirely in off-the-shelf 3D software, pushing character design into visceral and tender registers. Uses his own body and voice as reference; collaboration with musicians structures much of his output.
jesse kanda.commons_summary: Commercial/collaborative practice; work distributed primarily through music-industry and institutional channels.
jesse kanda.governance_summary: Solo practitioner operating across music-video industry and contemporary art.

jon rafman.practice_summary: Canadian artist whose 'Nine Eyes of Google Street View' (2008-) screen-grabs urban and landscape anomalies from the platform, foundational to post-internet practice. Subsequent work uses virtual tour, game engine, and CGI to stage online subcultures and their affective debris.
jon rafman.methodology: Harvests and curates from platforms — Google Street View, 4chan, Second Life — rather than generating from scratch. Later works assemble found and commissioned CGI into long-form video and VR installations. Controversy around allegations (2020) has shaped institutional reception.
jon rafman.commons_summary: Practice built on re-presenting proprietary platform data; consent relationship to source material is part of the critical content.
jon rafman.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; represented by Sprüth Magers.

joshua davis.practice_summary: American designer-artist associated with early-2000s Flash-era web experimentation (Praystation, Once Upon a Forest). Ongoing practice uses generative process to produce prints, identity systems, and commercial design at the boundary between art and applied graphics.
joshua davis.methodology: Builds custom generative systems in Processing and HYPE (open-source framework he maintains). Workflow explicitly mixes commercial client work and autonomous art; documents process transparently.
joshua davis.commons_summary: HYPE Framework is open-source (released under MIT); Davis has long been an advocate of process-transparent practice.
joshua davis.governance_summary: Solo studio; maintains HYPE Framework as open-source project.

katja novitskova.practice_summary: Estonian artist whose sculptural practice — freestanding print cut-outs of animals sourced from stock imagery — treats the infrastructure of biological data and corporate 3D imaging as aesthetic and speculative material. 'Approximations' series is a canonical reference point in post-internet sculpture.
katja novitskova.methodology: Sources images from open biological databases, stock photography, and corporate-science archives. Transforms these into aluminium and paper cut-outs, installations, and video. Work sits at a speculative-realist register — treating species and platforms as entangled.
katja novitskova.commons_summary: Commercial gallery practice using largely public/open-source image material as substrate.
katja novitskova.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; represented by Kraupa-Tuskany Zeidler.

kevin mccoy.practice_summary: American artist who, with Anil Dash, minted 'Quantum' — widely recognised as the first NFT — on Namecoin in May 2014, predating the commercial NFT category by six years. Earlier practice in performance, collaboration, and curatorial work via Monegraph and his own collaborative platforms.
kevin mccoy.methodology: Long practice of treating digital provenance and artist-authored platforms as medium. Co-founded Monegraph (2014) to use blockchain for digital-art authentication; continues to make video and performance work.
kevin mccoy.commons_summary: Pre-boom work was technically experimental; 'Quantum' was auctioned at Sotheby's 2021. Ongoing interest in artist-authored provenance infrastructure.
kevin mccoy.governance_summary: Solo and collaborative (with Jennifer McCoy) practice; academic role at NYU Tisch.

kim asendorf.practice_summary: German artist whose pixel-sorting algorithms (2010) became foundational to glitch-art practice and were widely adopted across generative art in the 2010s. Later work explores on-chain generative art via fxhash and Art Blocks.
kim asendorf.methodology: Builds glitch and generative algorithms in Python/JavaScript; releases many as open-source. His pixel-sort algorithm and variants have been reimplemented thousands of times — a textbook case of generative infrastructure.
kim asendorf.commons_summary: Releases many works as open-source on GitHub; pixel-sort algorithm is deeply embedded in public creative-coding practice.
kim asendorf.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; platform-native (fxhash, Art Blocks, own releases).

lawrence lek.practice_summary: Malaysian-British artist whose 'Sinofuturism (1839-2046 AD)' essay-video and subsequent CGI world-building films — 'Geomancer', 'AIDOL', 'Black Cloud', 'NOX' — articulate a non-Western futurism through AI characters, architecture, and ambient soundtrack. Architectural training shapes his worlds at game-engine scale.
lawrence lek.methodology: Builds entire environments in Unreal Engine, composing architecture, AI-character scripts, and music for each film/installation. Often embeds his own ambient soundtracks. Treats the game engine as an authorial medium on par with cinema.
lawrence lek.commons_summary: Films are often released online in full after exhibition run; ambient soundtracks released via Bandcamp/Hyperdub.
lawrence lek.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; represented by Sadie Coles HQ.

lynn hershman leeson.practice_summary: American artist whose work since the 1960s has interrogated AI, bioart, surveillance, and gendered identity decades before each became canonical. 'Lorna' (1984) is widely recognised as the first interactive video art. Her CybeRoberta and DiNA projects staged AI agents as feminist art long before contemporary AI-art discourse.
lynn hershman leeson.methodology: Early adopter of every emerging technology (laser disc, networked chat, AI avatars, CRISPR) as feminist critical material. Combines installation, performance, video, and later bioart/DNA into long-arc projects spanning decades.
lynn hershman leeson.commons_summary: Career-long archive is preserved through Stanford University Libraries; ZKM mounted major 'Civic Radar' retrospective. Practice has always been public-facing and institutional.
lynn hershman leeson.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; long-standing institutional relationships (ZKM, Stanford, SFMOMA).

manfred mohr.practice_summary: German-American artist whose algorithmic practice since 1969 systematically explores the hypercube as generative substrate. One of the earliest sustained commitments to computer-drawn art as primary medium, from mechanical plotters to real-time displays.
manfred mohr.methodology: Develops algorithms based on n-dimensional hypercubes and their projections, executed first on CDC mainframes with Zuse Graphomat plotters, now on screens and custom displays. Produces series over decades — 'Cubic Limit', 'Divisibility', 'Klangfarben' — as sustained iterative research.
manfred mohr.commons_summary: Academic/gallery practice; source code for older works is slowly being archived through institutional partnerships.
manfred mohr.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; represented by bitforms gallery NYC.

matt deslauriers.practice_summary: Canadian generative artist whose 'Meridian' (2021) and 'Subscapes' Art Blocks releases, together with his open-source tool ecosystem (canvas-sketch, penplot), made him an infrastructure figure of 2020s on-chain generative art.
matt deslauriers.methodology: Writes generative algorithms with an emphasis on painterly or landscape-like output (noise fields, colour palettes, compositional rules). Maintains canvas-sketch as a widely-used open-source JS framework for generative art.
matt deslauriers.commons_summary: canvas-sketch (MIT-licensed) is widely used across creative-coding education and practice; active GitHub release cadence.

matt kane.practice_summary: American artist whose algorithmic painting practice bridges procedural generation and pictorial tradition. 'Gazers' (2021) introduced programmable art-as-token where lunar phases dynamically alter the image, a reference for on-chain mutability.
matt kane.methodology: Builds custom software that treats the painting surface as programmable — pixel operations, transformations tied to external data (moon, weather). Each token series develops a specific procedural language.
matt kane.commons_summary: Practice is commercial, but programmable-art format contributes a conceptual commons to the field — the 'art that responds to the world' pattern.

mitchell chan.practice_summary: Canadian conceptual artist and writer whose 'Digital Zones of Immaterial Pictorial Sensibility' (2017) was one of the earliest rigorous artistic engagements with blockchain — restaging Yves Klein's 1959 'Zones' via Ethereum smart contract.
mitchell chan.methodology: Works in dense conceptual restaging — reading contemporary digital-economic forms (smart contracts, DAOs, gas fees) through art-historical precedent. Writing is as much the work as the object. Active in FFT/Feral File contexts.
mitchell chan.commons_summary: Writing distributed openly (Outland, personal site); contracts are public on-chain.

nicolas jaar.practice_summary: Chilean-American musician, producer, and label founder whose practice links electronic music, politics, and moving image. As Against All Logic and under his own name, and through the Other People label, he has built a polyphonic output that crosses club, ambient, essay-film and radio.
nicolas jaar.methodology: Builds long-form albums, mixes, and radio-essays that refuse genre fixity. Work often sits at the intersection of memory, displacement, and political resistance (Chile, Palestine). Physical and digital releases coexist; extensive live-mix archive on Boiler Room and own platform.
nicolas jaar.commons_summary: Other People label shares an archival ethos; several works released as pay-what-you-can. Strong political-commons orientation.

olia lialina.practice_summary: Russian-German net.art pioneer whose 'My Boyfriend Came Back from the War' (1996) is a canonical work of the medium, and whose scholarly-preservationist work (with Dragan Espenschied on One Terabyte of Kilobyte Age) has shaped how the web's amateur history is remembered.
olia lialina.methodology: Works across HTML-native artwork, archival retrieval of GeoCities-era material, and scholarly writing on vernacular web aesthetics. Teaches at Merz Akademie Stuttgart. Practice treats the browser as authorial substrate and the amateur web as serious cultural record.
olia lialina.commons_summary: One Terabyte of Kilobyte Age is an open research archive; teaching is a core public-commons contribution. Strong preservation ethic.
olia lialina.governance_summary: Academic + artist practice (Merz Akademie, professor); independent net.art work.

petra cortright.practice_summary: American artist whose webcam self-portraits ('VVEBCAM', 2007) and Photoshop-process paintings became reference points in post-internet practice. The work sits at the seam between digital gesture, domestic feminine labour, and painterly tradition.
petra cortright.methodology: Records short webcam self-portraits using Photobooth-style effects; builds Photoshop files with hundreds of layers and prints them as digital paintings on aluminium. Practice insists on the digital gesture (clip-art, stock image) as native painterly material.
petra cortright.commons_summary: Earlier webcam work is distributed freely online (VVEBCAM on YouTube until deleted by Google); current practice is commercial gallery.
petra cortright.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; represented by Foxy Production.

primavera de filippi.practice_summary: Italian legal scholar and artist whose 'Plantoid' series (2015-) deployed blockchain as autonomous organism — DAOs that commission their own reproduction. Academic work on blockchain governance ('Blockchain and the Law', 2018) runs parallel to artistic practice.
primavera de filippi.methodology: Bridges legal scholarship, artistic research, and open-source code. Plantoids are sculptural-performance-legal hybrids: each receives Ether, commissions human artists to build the next generation. Co-founded Coalition of Automated Legal Applications (COALA).
primavera de filippi.commons_summary: Strongest-possible commons orientation — research published openly, COALA as open legal infrastructure, Plantoid as open-source art framework.
primavera de filippi.governance_summary: Academic (CNRS, Harvard Berkman Klein) + artist practice; COALA as multi-stakeholder consortium.

rafael lozano-hemmer.practice_summary: Mexican-Canadian artist whose large-scale participatory installations use biometric and sensor data to produce durational, public-facing artworks. 'Pulse Room', 'Voice Array', and the 'Pulse' series stage the crowd's pulse, voice, or shadow as collective data artwork.
rafael lozano-hemmer.methodology: Commissions or builds custom sensor-and-software stacks and deploys them at public/civic scale (plazas, galleries, museums). Source code for almost all works is released on GitHub ('antimodular' repository). Treats each piece as a technical publication as well as an artwork.
rafael lozano-hemmer.commons_summary: All source code published on GitHub under permissive licences; a rare case of a blue-chip interactive artist maintaining a full open-source practice.
rafael lozano-hemmer.governance_summary: Antimodular Research (studio collective in Montréal); gallery-represented (Pace, Bitforms).

rhea myers.practice_summary: British conceptual artist working with blockchain since 2011, among the earliest artists to treat the technology as conceptual medium rather than market. 'Is Art?', 'Secret Artwork', 'Tokens Equal Text' engage smart contracts as conceptual apparatus.
rhea myers.methodology: Writes Solidity/Ethereum contracts as conceptual works; maintains an explicitly leftist political orientation that reads blockchain critically. Writing ('Proof of Work', Urbanomic 2019) theorises the aesthetic-political stakes.
rhea myers.commons_summary: All contracts and writings published openly; many works are free-to-mint. Explicitly anti-commodification in practice and theory.
rhea myers.governance_summary: Solo practitioner / writer; published by Urbanomic.

robbie barrat.practice_summary: American artist who, as a teenager, open-sourced early GAN-based fine-art generators ('AI Generated Nude Portraits') that became reference material for the 2018-19 GAN-art moment — including, famously, work reused by Obvious for the Christie's sale without credit.
robbie barrat.methodology: Trained GANs on public art-history datasets (WikiArt, Jean-Michel Basquiat); released code and models on GitHub. Later practice includes refusal performances (auctioned NFT of an empty JPEG) and continues to circle the ethics of AI art and attribution.
robbie barrat.commons_summary: Early work distributed entirely via GitHub under permissive licences; foundational commons contribution to GAN art. Later practice more gallery-embedded.

robert hodgin.practice_summary: American generative artist whose practice since the late 2000s has explored flocking, fluid, and procedural terrain systems. 'Meander' (Art Blocks Curated, 2021) renders imagined maps of rivers and settlements; a widely-referenced work in on-chain generative art.
robert hodgin.methodology: Builds systems in Cinder (C++), then later JavaScript/WebGL for on-chain compatibility. Strong interest in naturalistic emergent simulation — rivers, crowds, atmosphere.
robert hodgin.commons_summary: Long-time contributor to Cinder (open-source C++ creative-coding framework).

sarah zucker.practice_summary: American artist working across analogue video synthesis, animation, and NFT. Uses vintage broadcast equipment (CRT, Sony AVC video synthesiser) to produce hand-made digital-analogue hybrid works on VHS, later minted on chain.
sarah zucker.methodology: Treats analogue video as living archive — synthesising, recording to tape, then digitising and minting. Practice is deeply material despite ending in on-chain tokens. Active writer on crypto art as well.
sarah zucker.commons_summary: Shares technical methodology openly (analogue video signal chain); gallery-commercial practice otherwise.

simon denny.practice_summary: New Zealand-born artist whose installations stage the architecture of technology capitalism — server farms, patent filings, seasteading diagrams, crypto-mining rigs. 'Mine' (2019) and 'Security Through Obscurity' interrogate the political-economic infrastructures digital art typically renders invisible.
simon denny.methodology: Extensive journalistic-research phase (industry interviews, patent searches, corporate archives) feeds installation and printed matter. Collaborates with academics, journalists, and designers to present the findings as immersive installation.
simon denny.commons_summary: Extensively documented books (Serpentine / Mousse publications) place research into public circulation.
simon denny.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; represented by Petzel Gallery and others.

snowfro.practice_summary: Erick Calderon, founder of Art Blocks (2020) — the on-chain generative art platform that instantiated a new category of blockchain-native digital art. His own project 'Chromie Squiggle' (2020) is the platform's canonical first piece and remains its symbolic centre.
snowfro.methodology: Built Art Blocks as platform infrastructure and houses his own 'Chromie Squiggle' as the default generative work minted by collectors as the platform's genesis. Runs Art Blocks as full-time infrastructure role; own artistic output is more occasional.
snowfro.commons_summary: Art Blocks open-sources its smart contracts and artist documentation; artist contracts embed terms that keep the generative code accessible.
snowfro.governance_summary: Founder and operator of Art Blocks (commercial platform); individual practice is secondary to platform role.

sondra perry.practice_summary: American artist whose CGI-and-installation practice interrogates the racial politics of digital tools — default skin tones, Blender avatar defaults, hospital software, the colour blue as surveillance substrate. 'Typhoon coming on', 'Resident Evil', and 'Lineage for a Multiple Monitor Workstation' are canonical works.
sondra perry.methodology: Uses consumer and institutional digital tools (Blender, exercise bikes, chroma-key blue) against themselves, staging the politics built into their defaults. Installations combine video, interactive elements, and deliberately cheap-feeling office furniture as institutional critique.
sondra perry.commons_summary: Commercial gallery practice; some writings and talks distributed openly.

trevor paglen.practice_summary: American artist and geographer whose work maps the infrastructures of surveillance, covert military operation, and machine vision. 'Limit Telephotography', 'The Other Night Sky', 'ImageNet Roulette' (with Kate Crawford), and 'Orbital Reflector' stage these as photograph, dataset audit, and sky-sculpture respectively.
trevor paglen.methodology: Field-research practice — long-lens photography of black sites, FOIA requests, analysis of classified patches, AI-system forensics. Often collaborates with scholars (Kate Crawford, Nick Mirzoeff). Each body of work doubles as investigative-journalism output.
trevor paglen.commons_summary: Investigative-scholarly outputs published openly (Excavating AI with Crawford, 'Invisible Images'); artworks are gallery-commercial.
trevor paglen.governance_summary: Solo practitioner with long-standing academic collaborators; PhD in geography.

tyler hobbs.practice_summary: American generative artist whose 'Fidenza' (2021) Art Blocks Curated release reframed long-form generative art for the blockchain era and became, by market and critical reception, one of the category-defining works of on-chain generative art.
tyler hobbs.methodology: Writes JavaScript algorithms generating painterly compositions — flow fields, colour palettes, compositional variation. Writes extensively on generative aesthetics ('Aesthetically Programming', essays) and has helped shape the conceptual vocabulary of the field.
tyler hobbs.commons_summary: Writing and educational materials distributed openly; commercial practice otherwise.
tyler hobbs.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; represented by Pace Gallery.

vera molnar.practice_summary: Hungarian-French artist (1924-2023) who is one of the earliest and most rigorous practitioners of computer art. Began using computers in 1968 after decades of combinatorial painting; continued producing algorithmically-derived work for over five decades. Co-founded the GRAV and Art et Informatique groups.
vera molnar.methodology: Began with 'machine imaginaire' — computing algorithms by hand before computers were available — and moved to FORTRAN and plotters in 1968. Long-running series iterate small rule changes across hundreds of variations, treating algorithm as durational material.
vera molnar.commons_summary: Academic/gallery practice; late-career retrospectives have placed her work in public-museum collections widely.
vera molnar.governance_summary: Solo practitioner throughout career; recognised via major European institutions in her final decade.

vuk cosic.practice_summary: Slovenian net.art founding figure who coined (or popularised) the term 'net.art' in 1996, and whose ASCII-movie series ('Deep ASCII' version of Deep Throat, etc.) are canonical works. Directed the Slovenian pavilion at Venice Biennale 2001 — the first Biennale pavilion dedicated to net.art.
vuk cosic.methodology: Works the limits of internet protocols and old-media translation — ASCII cinema, history of net.art documentation, curatorial-archival work. Deeply interwoven with the founding net.art group (Shulgin, Lialina, JODI, Bunting).
vuk cosic.commons_summary: All net.art works freely accessible; archival and curatorial work is an ongoing public contribution.
vuk cosic.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; institutionally embedded via Ljubljana's Ljudmila (net-culture lab).

xcopy.practice_summary: Pseudonymous British artist whose GIF-based crypto-art aesthetic — flickering, glitched, skull-themed — became a defining visual language for the 2020-2022 NFT moment. 'Right-click and Save As guy' remains one of the canonical crypto-art works.
xcopy.methodology: Works in short looping GIFs using a narrow, instantly-legible visual palette — stuttering frames, high-contrast colour, textual fragments. Practice is strictly pseudonymous; personality surfaces only through output and chat presence.
xcopy.commons_summary: Work is platform-native (SuperRare, Nifty Gateway); commercial rather than commons-oriented but deeply shaped the shared iconography of crypto art.

zach lieberman.practice_summary: American artist and educator who co-created openFrameworks (2005-), the C++ creative-coding toolkit, and whose daily-sketch practice on Instagram has shaped the visual vocabulary of interactive typography and real-time graphics.
zach lieberman.methodology: Daily-sketch discipline — one short real-time graphics experiment per day, posted publicly. Works at the intersection of interactive typography, sensor input, and gesture. Co-founded the School for Poetic Computation (SFPC) in 2013.
zach lieberman.commons_summary: openFrameworks is MIT-licensed, deeply embedded in creative-coding practice worldwide. SFPC is a major experimental-pedagogy contribution to the field.
zach lieberman.governance_summary: Solo artistic practice + pedagogical/infrastructural roles (SFPC, openFrameworks community). Faculty at MIT Media Lab.

kenneth knowlton.practice_summary: American computer scientist and artist (1931-2022) who, at Bell Labs, pioneered computer animation (BEFLIX language, 1963) and the computer-graphic mosaic. 'Studies in Perception I' (1966) with Leon Harmon — a nude reassembled from electronic symbols — is one of the foundational works of computer art.
kenneth knowlton.methodology: Developed BEFLIX (Bell Flicks) and later EXPLOR at Bell Labs; built mosaic-rendering algorithms using seashells, dominoes, and other physical tokens to encode images. Long academic and industrial-research practice at the beginning of computer graphics.
exhibitions: The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age (MoMA 1968)
kenneth knowlton.commons_summary: Industrial-research practice; BEFLIX and related tools were internal Bell Labs systems, but the art-historical output has been publicly documented and exhibited across generations.
kenneth knowlton.governance_summary: Bell Labs career researcher; artworks distributed through museum and academic channels.

mario klingemann.practice_summary: German artist whose two-decade practice in AI-based image-making predates the 2022 diffusion-model boom. 'Memories of Passersby I' (2018) is one of the first autonomous GAN-based artworks purchased by a major gallery (Sotheby's); extensive output spans neural-style transfer, GAN portraiture, and diffusion-era practice.
mario klingemann.methodology: Writes, trains, and fine-tunes neural models — often on self-assembled datasets — and runs them as autonomous systems. Publishes models and intermediate outputs on GitHub/Twitter; long-running practice of 'doing public R&D'.
mario klingemann.commons_summary: Long history of publishing models, code, and datasets openly; significant educational-commons contribution to the AI-art field.

reza negarestani.practice_summary: Iranian philosopher and writer whose theory-fiction 'Cyclonopedia' (2008) and subsequent rationalist-philosophical work ('Intelligence and Spirit', 2018) are heavily cited across digital-art and speculative-philosophy contexts. His writing functions for many practitioners as primary theoretical material.
reza negarestani.methodology: Writes theory-fiction and systematic philosophy that blurs scholarly and speculative registers. Foundational influence on current thinking about AI, intelligence, and the computational.
reza negarestani.commons_summary: Extensively published through Urbanomic and academic presses; much writing accessible online. Work is heavily cited in digital-art theoretical discourse.
reza negarestani.governance_summary: Academic/independent philosopher; currently faculty at The New Centre for Research & Practice.

alexei shulgin.practice_summary: Russian net.art founding figure — part of the original circle with Olia Lialina, Vuk Ćosić, JODI, and Heath Bunting — whose 1990s works treated the web as critical and formal medium. Later practice with 386DX staged the obsolescent PC as performance instrument; ongoing curatorial role in the Moscow net-culture scene.
alexei shulgin.methodology: Works across net.art object, performance, and curatorial practice. 'Form Art Competition' (1997) and the 'Easylife.org' platform instantiate the web-as-artwork argument foundational to net.art.
alexei shulgin.commons_summary: All net.art works remain freely accessible; Easylife.org is an artist-run public archive of early net.art.
alexei shulgin.governance_summary: Independent practitioner; involved with MediaArtLab Moscow.

auriea harvey.practice_summary: American-Belgian artist whose practice spans three eras of digital art: late-90s net.art (Entropy8Zuper!), 2000s independent games (Tale of Tales, with Michaël Samyn), and current decade digital sculpture, VR, and NFT. Few practitioners have as continuous a digital-native practice across media generations.
auriea harvey.methodology: Each era defines its own methodology: Entropy8 was HTML-native narrative-surreal; Tale of Tales produced art games ('The Path', 'The Graveyard') as self-contained experiences; current practice builds 3D sculptures distributed across physical, digital, and NFT form, often referencing classical sculpture's history.
auriea harvey.commons_summary: Net.art era distributed freely; Tale of Tales games were commercial; current practice mixes gallery, NFT, and open 3D-model release.
auriea harvey.governance_summary: Solo/duo practice throughout; currently represented by bitforms.

bernard stiegler.practice_summary: French philosopher (1952-2020) whose 'Technics and Time' trilogy and subsequent work on attention, pharmacology, and automation are foundational to digital-art theory. Founded Ars Industrialis and Institut de Recherche et d'Innovation (IRI) at Centre Pompidou.
bernard stiegler.methodology: Combined speculative philosophy with institutional practice — IRI at Pompidou developed annotation-and-study tools treating attention as political and economic material. His concepts (tertiary retention, general organology, pharmakon) recur widely in contemporary digital-arts theory.
bernard stiegler.commons_summary: IRI and Ars Industrialis produced open software and public-thinking infrastructure. Publications are widely translated and distributed.
bernard stiegler.governance_summary: Academic philosopher (Compiègne, Pompidou IRI, Ars Industrialis).

carsten nicolai alva noto.practice_summary: German artist and musician whose dual practice as Carsten Nicolai (installation, sculpture, visual art) and Alva Noto (electronic music, Raster-Noton label) has shaped both audio-visual installation art and contemporary electronic music since the late 1990s.
carsten nicolai alva noto.methodology: Works the formal limits of sine waves, clicks, and visual-audio synchronisation. Raster-Noton (founded 1996) operates as both label and aesthetic position. Frequent large-scale installation collaborations at Documenta, Venice Biennale. Long-running duo work with Ryuichi Sakamoto until the latter's death.
carsten nicolai alva noto.commons_summary: Raster-Noton releases are commercial but curated at label level; artistic practice is gallery-embedded.
carsten nicolai alva noto.governance_summary: Solo dual-identity practice; co-runs Raster-Noton label (with Olaf Bender and previously Frank Bretschneider).

cornelia sollfrank.practice_summary: German feminist net-artist and theorist, co-founder of the Old Boys Network (1997, the first cyberfeminist collective). Practice combines artwork ('Female Extension', 1997), academic research (PhD on generative art and authorship), and activism.
cornelia sollfrank.methodology: 'Female Extension' submitted 289 fake female artists to a net-art competition to expose the gender gap in curated net-art shows. Subsequent practice treats authorship itself as contested site — generative net-art, writings on piracy, commons, and feminist tech.
exhibitions: Zentrum für Kunst und Medien Karlsruhe (ZKM)
cornelia sollfrank.commons_summary: Long-running commitment to commons/piracy/feminist-tech discourse; writing and research are public-facing. Academic role at HFBK Hamburg.
cornelia sollfrank.governance_summary: Independent / academic practice; OBN operated as artist-led collective.

darius kazemi.practice_summary: American artist, programmer, and writer whose bot-art practice (under tinysubversions) pioneered Twitter-era computational creativity. Co-founded NaNoGenMo (National Novel Generation Month) in 2013 and Mastodon instance Friend Camp as community-infrastructure practice.
darius kazemi.methodology: Prolific output of bots, generators, and small tools — 'Tiny Subversions' blog and GitHub are the primary venue. Recent practice focuses on small-scale decentralised social infrastructure (Mastodon, Hometown fork).
darius kazemi.commons_summary: Deep commons orientation — essentially everything is open-source on GitHub, including platform experiments (Hometown Mastodon fork).
darius kazemi.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; active in federated-social-web commons.

dragan espenschied.practice_summary: German artist and digital preservationist, preservation director at Rhizome (New York) and member of the net-art duo Bodenständig 2000. Has been central to institutional-scale digital art preservation via Webrecorder / Conifer and the Emulation-as-a-Service Infrastructure.
dragan espenschied.methodology: Splits practice between preservation infrastructure (Webrecorder tooling, Rhizome's emulation stack) and archival-artistic work. With Olia Lialina, maintains 'One Terabyte of Kilobyte Age' — a slow Twitter/Tumblr screenshot feed of archived GeoCities pages.
dragan espenschied.commons_summary: Webrecorder and Conifer are open-source; One Terabyte of Kilobyte Age is open cultural research.
dragan espenschied.governance_summary: Preservation director at Rhizome (non-profit); duo practice with Olia Lialina.

georg nees.practice_summary: German mathematician and artist (1926-2016) whose February 1965 exhibition at Studiengalerie Stuttgart of plotter drawings generated on a Siemens computer is widely cited as the first exhibition of computer-generated art. His PhD 'Generative Computergrafik' (1969, supervised by Max Bense) is a foundational text of the field.
georg nees.methodology: Programmed ALGOL on the Siemens 2002, outputting to a Zuse Graphomat Z64 pen plotter. Treated the algorithm as aesthetic substrate — the same procedural impulse that Frieder Nake shared; the two are closely associated. Industrial career at Siemens ran parallel to academic-artistic output.
georg nees.commons_summary: Industrial-academic practice; Compart database (University of Bremen, maintained by Nake) preserves many of Nees's works as public scholarly archive.
georg nees.governance_summary: Industrial research career at Siemens; academic-artistic output exhibited and archived through Stuttgart-Bremen-ZKM network.

giorgio moscati.practice_summary: Brazilian physicist and early computer-art pioneer. Collaborated with Waldemar Cordeiro in the late 1960s on some of the earliest computer-art works produced in Latin America, connecting Brazilian concrete art's rigorous formalism with nascent computer graphics.
giorgio moscati.methodology: As a physicist at the University of São Paulo, provided the computational infrastructure for Cordeiro's visual experiments, using mainframe computers in ways structurally similar to the Stuttgart and Bell Labs milieux but within a distinct Latin American concrete-arts lineage.
giorgio moscati.commons_summary: Academic practice; output relatively sparse but culturally significant for non-Euro-American early-computer-art coverage.
giorgio moscati.governance_summary: Academic (University of São Paulo) with occasional artistic collaboration.
giorgio moscati.confidence_note: Limited English-language documentation; biographical details thin. Profile constructed from available scholarly references on Cordeiro's computational turn.

iannis xenakis.practice_summary: Greek-French composer, architect, and mathematician (1922-2001) whose stochastic composition methods and the UPIC graphical composition system (1977) made him a foundational figure in computer music. UPIC — which allowed composers to draw sonic structures that the computer then realised — is one of the defining tools of algorithmic music.
iannis xenakis.methodology: Developed stochastic composition using probability distributions (Gaussian, Poisson, Markov chains) starting in the 1950s, initially computed by hand. UPIC was developed at CEMAMu, the computer-music research centre he founded. Deep entanglement with Le Corbusier's architectural practice informed his spatialised composition.
iannis xenakis.commons_summary: UPIC was academic-institutional; Xenakis's writings ('Formalized Music') are widely distributed. CCMIX (now Centre Iannis Xenakis) continues as public institution.
iannis xenakis.governance_summary: Academic / institutional practice (CEMAMu, Indiana University); legacy maintained by Centre Iannis Xenakis.

ken perlin.practice_summary: American computer graphics researcher whose Perlin noise algorithm (1983), developed for 'Tron', won an Academy Award for Technical Achievement in 1997 and became foundational infrastructure underlying most procedural content generation in games, film VFX, and generative art.
ken perlin.methodology: Academic research practice — NYU Media Research Lab, Future Reality Lab. Publishes algorithms openly; Perlin noise and its successors (simplex noise, curl noise) are unencumbered by patent and free-to-use, a deliberate decision.
exhibitions: (not applicable — researcher, though his algorithm underlies countless exhibited works)
ken perlin.commons_summary: Perlin noise is an enormous commons contribution — structurally fundamental to generative art's present form.
ken perlin.governance_summary: Academic (NYU) computer-graphics researcher; director of NYU Future Reality Lab.

laturbo avedon.practice_summary: Avatar-artist practicing entirely as a virtual persona since 2012 — the artist is the avatar; there is no 'real' identity behind it. Work across CGI animation, social media performance, and commissioned games foregrounds digital-native identity as primary material.
laturbo avedon.methodology: Maintains avatar-consistent presence across platforms (Instagram, Twitter, commissioned work, gallery). Produces CGI animations and collaborations with musicians, brands, and institutions; the persona itself is part of the work's governance.
laturbo avedon.commons_summary: Practice is avatar-native — commercial gallery, commissioned brand work, and institutional commission. Identity is the primary critical gesture.
laturbo avedon.governance_summary: Single persistent avatar-practice; represented by Transfer Gallery.

lev manovich.practice_summary: Russian-American theorist whose 'The Language of New Media' (2001) is the single most cited scholarly text in digital-art theory. Subsequent work on cultural analytics, software studies, and AI has sustained his foundational position across three decades.
lev manovich.methodology: Writes across book-length scholarship, software-studies toolmaking (Cultural Analytics Lab at CUNY), and visual-data projects. Moves between theory and empirical large-scale visual analysis of cultural datasets (Instagram, Flickr, movie frames).
lev manovich.commons_summary: Cultural Analytics Lab publishes tools and datasets openly; 'The Language of New Media' is required reading across digital-art curricula.
lev manovich.governance_summary: Academic (CUNY Graduate Center); director of Cultural Analytics Lab.

lu yang.practice_summary: Chinese multimedia artist whose gender-fluid avatar-based practice draws on Buddhist iconography, medical imaging, anime, and game engines. Represented China at Venice Biennale 2015; won Deutsche Bank Artist of the Year 2022.
lu yang.methodology: Builds elaborate CGI universes centred around 'DOKU' — a non-binary digital incarnation — distributed across video, installation, game, music video, and live performance. Collaborates with musicians, animation studios, and game-engine specialists.
lu yang.commons_summary: Gallery-commercial practice; some music-videos circulated widely on platforms.
lu yang.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; represented by Société Berlin, Edouard Malingue (now Kiang Malingue).

luciana parisi.practice_summary: Italian philosopher whose 'Contagious Architecture' (2013) and 'Abstract Sex' (2004), together with her current work on alien intelligence and computational reason, form a major theoretical reference in contemporary digital-arts and AI discourse. Professor of Literature, Art History, and Gender Studies at Duke.
luciana parisi.methodology: Works at the junction of computational theory, gender studies, and speculative philosophy. Dense, long-arc theoretical projects that move from biology (Abstract Sex) to algorithms (Contagious Architecture) to machine reasoning.
luciana parisi.commons_summary: Extensive public-facing academic output; frequent lecturer across art-school and institutional contexts.

mark fell.practice_summary: British artist and musician whose algorithmic sound practice — as half of SND since 1996, and solo since — has been central to the Mego/Editions Mego and Sheffield-electronic circles. Writing and theoretical work extend the practice into academic and curatorial territory.
mark fell.methodology: Uses custom algorithmic processes (often Max/MSP) to produce strict-rule compositions — stutter, modulation, rhythmic abstraction. Performs live with laptop; recorded output on Mego, Raster-Noton, The Death of Rave. Critical writing appears in The Wire, MIT Press, journals.
mark fell.commons_summary: Much theoretical writing available openly; music is commercial-label but on commons-adjacent independents.
mark fell.governance_summary: Solo/duo practice; academic role (University of Huddersfield / Plymouth).

mark tribe.practice_summary: American artist and educator who founded Rhizome in 1996 — the organisation that has more than any other institutionalised net.art and digital-art preservation. His own artistic practice includes 'Port Huron Project' (2006-8), a re-enactment of New Left speeches in situ.
mark tribe.methodology: Institution-building as primary practice (Rhizome), alongside photography, video, and re-enactment art. Tribe led Rhizome's early years of net-art acquisition and exhibition, building the infrastructure that shaped how net.art entered museum collections.
mark tribe.commons_summary: Rhizome is the landmark commons-oriented digital-art institution; Tribe's own later projects have mostly been open-access.

mendi + keith obadike.practice_summary: American married duo whose practice since the late 1990s spans net.art, sound installation, concert work, and writing. 'Blackness for Sale' (2001) auctioned Keith Obadike's blackness on eBay — a canonical net.art work on racial identity and platform commerce.
mendi + keith obadike.methodology: Works across multiple registers: net.art, sound installation, concert/opera (TREE OF FLOWERS, THE PLAYERS 2019), and scholarly writing (both are academics). Practice combines conceptual-art lineage with sustained engagement with African-American music, literature, and digital form.
mendi + keith obadike.commons_summary: Net.art works remain freely accessible; academic writing widely distributed. Concert work is institutional.
mendi + keith obadike.governance_summary: Duo practice; both hold academic roles.

mongrel.practice_summary: British net.art collective (1995-2010), founded by Graham Harwood, Mervin Jarman, Matsuko Yokokoji, and Richard Pierre-Davis. Their work interrogated race, class, and the digital divide through online tools and installation; 'National Heritage' (1996) and 'Color Separation' (2000s) are key works.
mongrel.methodology: Developed tools (Linker, social-software platforms) that were distributed to marginalised communities; the tools were themselves the artwork. Deliberately worked outside mainstream gallery circuit. Mongrel's members continued in successor formations (YoHa — Harwood and Yokokoji).
mongrel.commons_summary: Tools released openly; deep commitment to the commons and community-tech traditions.
mongrel.governance_summary: Artist collective; disbanded ~2010, successor practice continued as YoHa.

nora khan.practice_summary: American writer, editor, and curator whose critical work on digital and AI art — across Rhizome, Flash Art, Mousse, Aperture — has shaped the critical vocabulary of the past decade. Curated 'Fear of Content' and major AI-art exhibitions; editor at Rhizome and adjunct at Rhode Island School of Design.
nora khan.methodology: Writes long-form criticism, teaches, and curates. Maintains a position that is technically-informed but politically-attentive — a rare combination. Co-edited key volumes on AI art and sound.
exhibitions: (curator of multiple major exhibitions; not primarily an exhibiting artist)
nora khan.commons_summary: Criticism published widely and often open-access; teaching is core public contribution.
nora khan.governance_summary: Independent writer and curator; academic role at RISD.

peter ablinger.practice_summary: Austrian composer whose algorithmic-phonographic practice — 'Voices and Piano' transcribes famous voices into piano pulses; 'Talking Piano' makes a player-piano speak — occupies a unique position in contemporary computer music. Works also include site-specific sound installation and instrumental composition.
peter ablinger.methodology: Algorithmic transcription of extra-musical material (speech, noise, landscape) into instrumental form. Uses player-piano, strict compositional systems, and deep conceptual framing. Strong theoretical writing accompanies the work.
peter ablinger.commons_summary: Extensive scores and writings distributed via his own site; new-music-institutional rather than purely commercial.
peter ablinger.governance_summary: Independent composer; university teaching roles (Kunstuniversität Graz, Berlin).

robert mallary.practice_summary: American artist (1917-1997) who pioneered computer sculpture in the late 1960s, using IBM mainframes to generate 3D forms that were then realised in physical sculpture. 'Quad III' (1968) is one of the first computer-assisted sculptures.
robert mallary.methodology: Wrote programmes to generate 3D geometric forms as stacked cross-sections, which were then manually cut and assembled. Bridged from earlier assemblage and junk-sculpture practice into computational methods. Long teaching career at UMass Amherst.
robert mallary.commons_summary: Academic practice; archival material held at UMass Amherst.

russell haswell.practice_summary: British experimental sound artist whose computer-music and noise practice since the 1990s has been central to the Warp / Editions Mego scene. 'Live Salvage' (2001), collaborations with Florian Hecker, and his own work on extreme computer-music synthesis are reference points.
russell haswell.methodology: Uses custom algorithmic synthesis, extreme-dynamic-range sound, and performance-as-event. Often collaborates with visual artists and other sound practitioners; central to Yasunao Tone, Aphex Twin, Russell Haswell / Florian Hecker axis.
russell haswell.commons_summary: Releases are commercial but via independent/experimental labels (Warp, Editions Mego).

ruth catlow furtherfield.practice_summary: British artist and co-founder (with Marc Garrett) of Furtherfield (1997), one of the longest-running artist-led digital-arts organisations. Her practice spans artist-run platform development, commissioned work on blockchain/DAO art, and scholarly writing.
ruth catlow furtherfield.methodology: Combines artist-led organising (Furtherfield Gallery, Finsbury Park; Furtherfield Commons), commissioning, scholarly writing (co-editor of 'Artists Re:Thinking the Blockchain'), and own artistic practice in collaboration with partners.
ruth catlow furtherfield.commons_summary: Furtherfield is a flagship commons-oriented digital-arts organisation; extensive open publishing and commissioning.
ruth catlow furtherfield.governance_summary: Furtherfield operates as non-profit (UK charity); co-director model.

susan schuppli.practice_summary: Canadian artist-researcher and member of Forensic Architecture since 2011. 'Material Witness' (2020 book; exhibition) theorises how matter — ice cores, blood stains, oil spills — can bear testimony. Directs Centre for Research Architecture at Goldsmiths.
susan schuppli.methodology: Combines forensic-investigative methods with video essay, installation, and academic writing. Long-form projects span climate, conflict, and technology; each work functions as both artwork and evidentiary research.
susan schuppli.commons_summary: Research outputs often open-access (MIT Press publications, video essays on YouTube); academic commons strong.
susan schuppli.governance_summary: Director of Centre for Research Architecture, Goldsmiths; member of Forensic Architecture research agency.

constant.practice_summary: Constant is a Brussels-based non-profit artist-run association (vzw) active since 1997, focused on art, media, and technology through a feminist and free-libre lens. Known for sustained commitment to free-software culture, collaborative authorship, and events like the Libre Graphics Meeting.
constant.methodology: Works by organising sustained research-publication-performance cycles (Worksessions) with artists, programmers, and theorists. Outputs include publications, software experiments, and long-running archival infrastructure, released under free/libre licences.
constant.commons_summary: Core identity is commons-oriented — almost all output is published under free-culture licences (GPL, CC BY-SA, AGPL).
constant.governance_summary: Non-profit artist association (vzw) with rotating coordination and collective-governance ethos.
constant.confidence_note: Assumed the stub refers to Constant vzw (Brussels). Disambiguation flagged per spec.
